bib.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions

question: How can a black-box model's prediction be traced back through the learning algorithm to the training points most responsible for it?
hypothesis: Influence-function approximations stay useful on non-convex and non-differentiable models even though the theory assumes twice-differentiable, strictly convex risk.
contributions: Scalable influence-function computation using only gradients and Hessian-vector products (CG or stochastic Taylor-series estimation)
Empirical check that influence approximates leave-one-out retraining, including non-convex and smoothed non-differentiable losses
Applications: model comparison, visually-indistinguishable training-set attacks, domain-mismatch debugging, fixing mislabeled examples

method.summary: Computes I_up,loss(z,z_test) = -grad L(z_test)^T H^-1 grad L(z) with implicit Hessian-vector products (conjugate gradients or the Agarwal et al. stochastic estimator) and compares it with actual leave-one-out retraining. Uses it for case studies on MNIST, ImageNet dog-vs-fish, hospital readmission and Enron spam.

datasets.name: ImageNet dog vs fish
datasets.size: 900 training examples per class (1,800 total); 600 test images

datasets.name: Hospital readmission (diabetic patients)
datasets.size: balanced training set of 20K patients, 100+ US hospitals, 127 features
datasets.preprocessing: 30-day readmission label; 20 of 24 non-readmitted children under 10 removed to induce domain mismatch

datasets.name: Enron1 spam
datasets.preprocessing: bag-of-words; labels of a random 10% of training data flipped

models.name: CNN (MNIST)
models.architecture: 7 sets of conv layers, tanh, modeled on all-convolutional net (Springenberg et al.)

models.name: Inception v3, top layer trained
models.architecture: CNN with all but top layer frozen (equivalent to logistic regression on bottleneck features)

training.objective: empirical risk (logistic loss / hinge / smooth hinge) for the models; influence itself is not trained
training.steps: 500k iterations (CNN); leave-one-out retraining from the trained parameters for 30k steps
training.regularisation: L2 0.01 (logistic regression); damping lambda = 0.01 added to the Hessian for the CNN

other.note: CNN had not converged: another 500k full-pass iterations reduced train loss from 0.14 to 0.12

inference.samples: Single arbitrarily chosen test point per influence plot; 40 repeats for the mislabel experiment

parameters.attack_iterations: 100 per test image, retraining after each iteration
parameters.complexity: O(np + rtp) for all training points

metrics.name: Pearson's R between predicted and actual change in test loss
metrics.definition: correlation of -1/n * I_up,loss(z,z_test) with L(z_test, theta_-z) - L(z_test, theta) after leave-one-out retraining

metrics.name: Flip rate of test predictions
metrics.definition: fraction of correctly classified test images whose prediction flips after perturbing k training images

metrics.name: Test accuracy and fraction of flipped labels detected vs fraction of training data checked
metrics.definition: checking points ranked by influence, train loss, or random

baselines: coefficient of the 'child' indicator in learned parameters
eval.protocol: Single test point per comparison, error bars over 40 repeats for the label-repair experiment; no significance tests.

results.claim: Stochastic influence estimate and CG match leave-one-out retraining on MNIST
results.setup: Logistic regression, 10-class MNIST, n = 55,000, r = 10 repeats, t = 5,000 iterations, one wrongly classified test point
results.quote: The stochastic approximation from Agarwal et al. (2016) was also accurate with r = 10 repeats and t = 5, 000 iter-

results.claim: Influence correlates with leave-one-out retraining even for a non-converged CNN
results.setup: CNN, 2,616 parameters, 10% of MNIST, 500k Adam iterations, damping 0.01, 100 most influential points, one test point
results.quote:
predicted and actual changes in loss were highly correlated (Pearson’s R
= 0.86, Fig 2-Right)

results.claim: Smooth hinge (t = 0.001) lets influence predict hinge-loss retraining
results.setup: Linear SVM, MNIST 1s vs 7s, 100 most influential points, one wrongly classified test point; raw hinge overestimates
results.note: R = 0.91 at t = 0.1 (Fig 3 caption); unsmoothed hinge was inaccurate with no R given.

results.claim: Single-training-image perturbations flip a majority of correct predictions
results.setup: Inception top layer, dog vs fish, 591 of 600 test images initially correct, one training image of 1,800 perturbed, alpha 0.02, 100 iterations, same 8-bit representation
results.quote:
We were able to do this on 335
(57%) of the 591 test images.

results.claim: Perturbing 2 training images flips 77% of the 591 test predictions
results.setup: As above, 2 training images perturbed per test image
results.quote:
we could ﬂip predictions on
77% of the 591 test images

results.claim: One perturbed training image flipped 16 of 30 test predictions when attacking jointly
results.setup: 30 test images of the first author's dog, joint attack maximizing average loss

results.claim: Influence singles out the 4 children as 30-40x as influential as the next examples
results.setup: Hospital readmission logistic regression, 20K balanced patients, 127 features; random misclassified child as test point
results.quote:
each of whom
were 30-40 times as inﬂuential as the next most inﬂuential

results.claim: Parameter inspection baseline fails: 14 of 127 features had larger coefficient than the child indicator
Influence ranking repairs flipped labels better than train loss or random
results.setup: Enron1 spam, 4,147 train / 1,035 test, logistic regression on bag of words, 10% labels flipped, 40 repeats; the paper gives no numeric accuracy in text (curves in Fig 6)

results.claim: Influence functions are local: global changes such as subpopulation effects are an open question

limits: Theory assumes twice-differentiable, strictly convex risk; non-convex nets need damping (lambda = 0.01) and non-differentiable losses need smoothing.
Validation is on small models: CNN 2,616 parameters on 10% of MNIST, logistic regression, and a frozen-Inception top layer; no large network.
Agreement with leave-one-out is shown on one arbitrarily picked test point per plot, and on the top 100-500 influential points only; the paper says other points follow 'similar trends'.
Influence measures local, infinitesimal upweighting; the authors say global changes like removing a subpopulation are an open question.
Attack on discrete data is not tested empirically; the authors expect training-set attacks to get harder as training data grows.
Hardware, runtime and seeds for most experiments are not stated; Hessian-vector cost is O(p) per product but wall-clock numbers are not given.

terms.definition: rate of change of the loss at a test point when a training point is upweighted by an infinitesimal epsilon: -grad L(z_test)^T H^-1 grad L(z)
